segments: ... took {OCR?} the miserable city.
They began persuading those who were in the courts
to come out,
and that no one would harm them,
but they should go down to the sea and go wherever they wished, along with their wives, their sons, and their daughters,
except that they should not take anything of their possessions with them.
And as soon as they opened the gates,
and the Arabs entered among them to guard the property in the courts, so that they should not take anything from it,
they saw there sons and daughters with faces like the moon,
and the Arabs laid hands on them.
The Franks, however, did not endure it,
but drew swords and daggers,
and fell upon one another,
and countless people were killed from both sides.
And they destroyed the splendid and magnificent city,
and they did not leave the Franks anywhere on this great seacoast where they might lay their head.
These things happened in the month of Nisan of that same year,
which is the year 1603 [of the Greeks].
Again, the Egyptians gathered, a people beyond number,
and came and encamped against Qal'at ar-Rum on the Euphrates River.
And they took this too in the space of twenty days,
and they killed, took captive, plundered, and bound countless sons and daughters.
And they took the Armenian Catholicos along with all the monks who were found with him,
and brought him with honor to Damascus on Saturday the 26th
of the month of Haziran of that same year;
and behold, he was there.
Others, however, say {OCR?}
that this was not so,
but that they crucified him,
and those with him they hung in irons,
and took them to Egypt;
and his affair is not yet verified {OCR?}.
And that which is certain is
that in Damascus, in wretchedness, while imprisoned, he ended his life.
And when this was confirmed among the Armenians,
they chose for themselves a suitable man,
and consecrated for themselves a Catholicos in his place,
and he made his seat at Sis of Cilicia.
Now when Gaykhatu attained dominion,
and the kingdom of the house of Magog was established for him,
he was occupied with nothing except prodigality, play, and debauchery.
And he had no other thought such as is necessary and urgent for kings,
except that he should acquire and domesticate the sons and daughters of the nobles,
and debauch with them without restraint and without shame.
